User said: Can you explain what a p-value means in statistics? | I replied: A p-value answers a specific, narrow question: *If there were truly no effect (the null hypothesis were true), how often would I see data at least as extreme as what I actually observed, just by chance?*

So a p-value of 0.03 means: assuming no real effect, you'd see results this extreme (or more so) about 3% of the time. It's a measure of how surprising your data would be *under the null hypothesis*.

A few things it is **not**, which are commonly confused:

- It is **not** the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
- It is **not** the probability that your results happened "by chance."
- It does **not** tell you the size or importance of an effect. A tiny, trivial effect can yield a small p-value with enough data.

The conventional threshold of 0.05 is a convention, not a law of nature. "Significant" in this technical sense just means "below the chosen threshold"—it doesn't mean "important."

User said: What is the difference between precision and recall in machine learning? | I replied: Precision and recall both measure how well a classifier performs, but they answer different questions about your predictions.

**Precision** asks: *Of all the cases I flagged as positive, how many were actually positive?*

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Positives}}$$

It penalizes false alarms. High precision means when your model says "yes," it's usually right.

**Recall** asks: *Of all the cases that were actually positive, how many did I catch?*

$$\text{Recall} = \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Negatives}}$$

It penalizes misses. High recall means your model finds most of the real positives.

**The tension between them:** You can usually trade one for the other. If you make your model flag positives more aggressively, you'll catch more real cases (higher recall) but also raise more false alarms (lower precision). Tighten it up to avoid false alarms, and you'll miss more real cases.

**Which matters more depends on the cost of each error type:**

- *Cancer screening:* You want high **recall**—missing a real case (false negative) is far worse than a false alarm that gets ruled out by further testing.
